s: Oklo Inc. DEF 14A filed 21 Apr 2026, beneficial ownership as of 6 Apr 2026; OKLO close $42.09, 21 Aug 2026
m: Sum of his own holdings in proxy footnote 3 - 691,533 direct, 656,483 GRAT, 1,000,000 GRAT No.2, 7,851,901 Family Trust, 506,807 GRAT No.3, 28,090 RSUs = 10,734,814 shares x $42.09
did: Co-founded Oklo in July 2013 out of MIT nuclear engineering to build the Aurora, a 15-75 MWe sodium-cooled fast microreactor that runs on recycled used fuel, and to sell electricity by contract rather than sell reactors; listed via Sam Altman's AltC SPAC in May 2024.
why: Oklo skipped the utility sales model that killed every other small-reactor startup. By owning and operating the plants and signing power purchase agreements with data centres, it captured the AI electricity shortage as revenue instead of waiting for a utility customer that never orders.
obst: The NRC denied Oklo's Aurora combined licence application in January 2022 for insufficient safety information, the first-ever custom-reactor application rejection, forcing a three-year rebuild of the licensing case before the company had any revenue at all.
turn: The January 2022 NRC denial: instead of quitting, Oklo re-entered through the DOE fuel-fabrication and Idaho National Laboratory siting route, which by 2024 gave it a site, fuel and a listed currency ahead of every rival.

s: Oklo Inc. DEF 14A filed 21 Apr 2026, beneficial ownership as of 6 Apr 2026; OKLO close $42.09, 21 Aug 2026
m: Sum of her own holdings in proxy footnote 3 - 658,039 direct, 689,479 GRAT, 1,000,000 GRAT No.2, 7,583,085 Family Trust, 474,011 GRAT No.3, 19,663 RSUs = 10,424,277 shares x $42.09
did: Co-founded Oklo in July 2013 with Jacob DeWitte after MIT nuclear engineering and has been Chief Operating Officer since inception, running the fuel-supply, siting and manufacturing build-out for the Aurora microreactor at Idaho National Laboratory.
why: She turned the fuel side into the moat. Securing DOE-allocated recovered used fuel from the EBR-II inventory gave Oklo a licensed feedstock nobody else had, so the company could promise delivery dates while competitors were still negotiating enrichment supply.
obst: Building a nuclear operating company with no revenue through the 2022 NRC denial and a decade of pre-licensing, while serving on the DOE Nuclear Energy Advisory Committee to keep the regulatory route for non-light-water reactors open at all.
turn: The May 2024 AltC merger, which converted a decade of unpaid regulatory work into a listed balance sheet just as hyperscaler power demand made firm baseload contracts biddable.

s: Lam Research DEF 14A filed 24 Sep 2025, ownership as of 5 Sep 2025; LRCX close $314.00, 21 Aug 2026
m: 1,481,175 beneficially owned less 616,410 exercisable options = 864,765 shares x $314 = $272M, plus intrinsic value of the six option tranches at strikes of $17.68 to $98.15 disclosed in the same proxy, about $165M
did: Joined Lam Research in June 2012 as COO when Lam bought Novellus, where he had spent 18 years, and became CEO in December 2018; drove Lam into high-aspect-ratio etch and ALD deposition, the two steps that gate 3D NAND layer counts and gate-all-around logic.
why: Etch and deposition are consumable-like: every added memory layer needs another pass, so Lam bills per layer rather than per fab. Archer bet the roadmap on vertical scaling just as NAND went from 32 to 300-plus layers, making Lam's revenue rise with device complexity, not wafer count.
obst: He took the CEO job in December 2018 after his predecessor resigned abruptly over conduct, in the middle of a memory downturn, then had to rewire the China business when US export controls in October 2022 cut off Lam's largest single growth market.
turn: The 2020-2022 shift of Lam's mix toward cryogenic and high-aspect-ratio etch tools for 3D NAND and DRAM capacitors, which let Lam hold share as EUV lithography spending moved value toward ASML.

s: Netskope Inc. DEF 14A filed 27 May 2026, ownership as of 31 Mar 2026; NTSK close $14.51, 21 Aug 2026
m: 25,850,122 Class B shares beneficially owned - 1,486,408 direct plus 22,288,889 in the 2012 Sanjay Beri and Ava Malla Revocable Trust and related holdings - x $14.51
did: Co-founded Netskope in October 2012 after eight years running Juniper's access and security unit, building a cloud security broker that inspects traffic to thousands of SaaS applications inline; it listed on Nasdaq in September 2025.
why: Netskope built its own private backbone of data centres rather than renting hyperscaler capacity, so inspecting encrypted SaaS traffic did not add the latency that made competitors unusable. Enterprises that had banned cloud apps could finally allow them under policy.
obst: Netskope stayed private for 13 years and raised over $1.4bn while Zscaler listed in 2018 and compounded a public multiple; Beri had to keep funding a capital-heavy global network through the 2022-2023 growth-software repricing without an exit.
turn: The 2019-2020 pivot from cloud access security broker to full SASE, bundling secure web gateway and zero-trust network access, which moved Netskope from a point product into the seat that replaces the branch firewall.

s: Cerebras Systems 424B4 IPO prospectus filed 14 May 2026, ownership as of 31 Mar 2026; CBRS close $196.13, 21 Aug 2026
m: 1,805,200 shares beneficially owned after the offering per the principal stockholders table x $196.13; excludes unvested equity
did: Joined Cerebras in June 2018 as SVP of engineering and operations and became COO in September 2023, owning the manufacturing of the Wafer Scale Engine - a single chip cut from an entire 300mm wafer - and the CS-series systems and datacentre build-out behind it.
why: Nobody had shipped a wafer-sized die because yield math says one defect kills the part. Mallick's operations work made redundancy-and-repair routing and the custom packaging, power and cooling manufacturable at TSMC, turning a physics demo into a product with a delivery schedule.
obst: Cerebras filed to go public in September 2024 and then sat for 20 months, hostage to a single customer, G42 of Abu Dhabi, and a CFIUS review of that relationship, before the S-1 was refreshed and the IPO finally priced at $185 in May 2026.
turn: The December 2025 master relationship agreement with OpenAI, including a $1bn working capital loan and a warrant, which replaced G42 concentration with an anchor inference customer and unlocked the listing.

s: Apple Inc. DEF 14A filed 8 Jan 2026, beneficial ownership table; AAPL close $309.35, 21 Aug 2026
m: 1,074,404 shares beneficially owned x $309.35 = $332M; excludes RSUs vesting more than 60 days after the table date and excludes three decades of prior share sales
did: Joined Apple from GE Plastics in August 1995 and ran product operations then operations, becoming Chief Operating Officer in July 2025; he built the supplier network that assembles roughly 200 million iPhones a year and moved US-bound iPhone assembly to India from 2017.
why: Apple's margin comes from operations, not design: prepaying suppliers for exclusive access to CNC machines, laser drills and camera modules locks rivals out of the components for a year. Khan ran that capital-deployment machine, which is why competitors cannot copy a launch quickly.
obst: He absorbed the 2020 pandemic shutdown of Chinese assembly, the 2021-2022 chip famine and the Zhengzhou Foxconn walkout, then had to stand up Indian and Vietnamese capacity fast enough to blunt tariff exposure without breaking iPhone launch dates.
turn: Succeeding Jeff Williams as COO in July 2025, which put the person who had spent a decade diversifying Apple out of single-country assembly in charge of the whole operation as tariffs made that the central risk.

s: Sanmina DEF 14A filed 23 Jan 2026, ownership as of 31 Dec 2025; SANM implied price $188.81 from $10.12bn market cap on 53.60m shares, 21 Aug 2026
m: 1,533,369 shares beneficially owned, including 212,870 in the Sola Family Trust, x $188.81 = $289M, plus a $12.9M non-qualified deferred compensation balance disclosed in the same proxy
did: Co-founded Sanmina in San Jose in 1980 as a printed circuit board shop and built it into a contract manufacturer with 35,000 employees in 20 countries and $8.1bn of fiscal 2025 revenue; he was CEO 1991-2017 and returned as chairman and CEO in August 2020.
why: Sanmina kept the vertically integrated pieces - backplanes, cables, enclosures, PCB fabrication - that every other contract manufacturer outsourced to chase asset-light margins. When supply chains broke in 2020-2022, owning those steps let Sanmina quote lead times rivals could not.
obst: The $6bn all-stock merger with SCI Systems in December 2001 doubled the company straight into the telecom equipment collapse; Sanmina spent years closing plants and writing down goodwill, and the shares never regained their 2000 peak until the AI infrastructure cycle.
turn: The 2020 return to the CEO chair, which reoriented Sanmina toward cloud and AI infrastructure, medical and defence work and took non-GAAP EPS from $3.61 in 2021 to $6.04 in fiscal 2025.

s: Alamar Biosciences 424B4 IPO prospectus filed 17 Apr 2026, ownership as of 1 Mar 2026; ALMR close $34.24, 21 Aug 2026
m: 6,207,834 shares beneficially owned, 9.0% after the offering, x $34.24 = $213M; the IPO priced at $17.00 so the stake has roughly doubled since listing
did: Co-founded Alamar in Fremont in May 2018 to commercialise NULISA, an immunoassay that pushes protein detection into the femtogram range so blood tests can read brain proteins; earlier he founded Advanced Cell Diagnostics, sold to Bio-Techne in 2016.
why: Proteomics rivals sold breadth - thousands of proteins at mediocre sensitivity. Alamar sold depth on the proteins that matter in plasma, particularly neurology markers present at a thousandth the concentration mass spectrometry can see, which is exactly what Alzheimer's blood tests need.
obst: He was launching a research-tools company into the 2022-2024 life-science instrument recession that halved Quanterix and forced Olink and SomaLogic into sales; academic and pharma capital budgets were frozen for the entire pre-revenue phase.
turn: The 2023 ARGO platform launch aimed at neurodegeneration panels, which rode the arrival of anti-amyloid drugs and blood-based Alzheimer's screening and took revenue up 195% in the year before the April 2026 IPO.

s: Central Garden & Pet DEF 14A filed 22 Dec 2025, ownership as of 15 Dec 2025; CENT $44.40 and CENTA $38.43 closes, 21 Aug 2026
m: 1,600,459 Class B plus 1,386,792 Common valued at the $44.40 voting-share close = $132.6M, plus 1,432,565 Class A at the $38.43 close = $55.1M, total about $188M
did: Founded Central Garden & Pet in 1980 as a lawn and garden distributor in the East Bay, took it public in 1993 and rolled up more than 60 brands - Pennington, Nylabone, Kaytee, Aqueon, Amdro - into a $3.1bn revenue supplier; CEO 1980-2003 and 2007-2013, chairman since.
why: He owned distribution before he owned brands. Controlling shelf placement at Home Depot, Walmart and PetSmart meant Central could buy small garden and pet brands cheaply and immediately triple their retail footprint, a spread no brand-only acquirer could match.
obst: Losing the Scotts distribution business in the late 1990s removed a huge share of revenue and forced Central to become a branded manufacturer instead of a distributor; he also had to hold a dual-class structure through repeated activist pressure over the non-voting Class A stock.
turn: The 1998-2000 break with Scotts, which pushed him to buy Pennington Seed and the pet brands outright and turned a low-margin distributor into a manufacturer with its own gross margin.

s: BILL Holdings DEF 14A filed 27 Oct 2025, ownership as of 20 Oct 2025; BILL close $47.82, 21 Aug 2026
m: 67,430 direct plus 1,708,749 in the Chung Lacerte Trust plus 753,281 in custodial trusts plus 980,592 exercisable options and RSUs = 3,510,052 shares x $47.82; excludes 205,000 foundation shares
did: Founded Bill.com in 2006 after selling PayCycle to Intuit, building software that automates accounts payable and receivable for small businesses and moves the money itself; it listed in December 2019 and now processes payments for close to half a million businesses.
why: He sold through accountants, not businesses. Signing the accounting firms that already controlled small-business back offices gave BILL a distribution channel with near-zero acquisition cost, and once a firm standardised on it the switching cost sat with the accountant, not the client.
obst: BILL spent its first decade as a slow-growing utility that nobody would fund at software multiples, then after listing had to defend the float business as interest income collapsed and Ramp and Brex attacked the spend-management side; Starboard Value took an activist stake by 2025.
turn: The 2021 acquisition of Divvy for $2.5bn, which bolted corporate cards and spend management onto the payables engine and turned BILL from an invoicing tool into the small-business money platform.

s: Marqeta DEF 14A filed 21 Apr 2026, ownership as of 15 Apr 2026; MQ close about $16.36, 21 Aug 2026
m: 1,968,537 plus 1,968,537 GRAT shares plus 33,650,852 held by The Gardner 2008 Living Trust = 37,587,926 pre-split shares, 9,396,982 after the 1-for-4 reverse split, x $16.36; excludes options and childrens trusts
did: Founded Marqeta in Oakland in 2010 and built modern card-issuing infrastructure - open APIs that let a company spin up virtual and physical payment cards and authorise each transaction in real time; it powers Block's Cash App Card, DoorDash and Klarna and listed in June 2021.
why: Legacy issuer processors ran overnight batch files. Marqeta's just-in-time funding decided at the moment of swipe whether and how much to fund a card, which is the only way instant-delivery payouts, buy-now-pay-later and expense controls work at all. That primitive had no substitute.
obst: Block alone drove the majority of Marqeta's revenue, and the December 2022 renewal cut pricing hard; the stock fell roughly 90% from its 2021 debut and the company took until 2026 to reverse split and reach GAAP profitability.
turn: The 2018-2020 Cash App Card ramp at Block, which took Marqeta from a niche processor to the rails behind one of the fastest-growing consumer card programmes in the US and made the IPO possible.

s: SiTime DEF 14A filed 15 Apr 2026, ownership as of 30 Mar 2026; SITM close $614.83, 21 Aug 2026
m: 210,696 shares beneficially owned, including family dynasty trusts and 9,208 near-term RSUs, x $614.83 = $130M; a floor, since it excludes a decade of disclosed sales
did: Took over SiTime as CEO in September 2007 after running Ikanos Communications, and spent eighteen years replacing quartz crystal oscillators with MEMS silicon timing devices; SiTime was sold to MegaChips for $200m in 2014, then spun back out in a November 2019 IPO.
why: Quartz oscillators cannot be shrunk, cannot survive shock and vibration and come from a fragile Japanese supply base. Silicon MEMS timing is programmable and made in a standard fab, so one part number replaced hundreds and datacentre and automotive customers got parts quartz vendors could not deliver.
obst: MEMS timing was a twenty-year graveyard of failed startups; SiTime ran out of venture money and had to sell itself to MegaChips in 2014 at $200m, and after the 2019 re-IPO revenue fell by a third in the 2023 inventory correction.
turn: Winning designed-in timing sockets in AI datacentre switching and optical modules from 2023, where jitter budgets are tight enough that quartz simply fails, which tripled revenue and took the stock past $600.
